analysis.one_liner: Bans mid-decade congressional redistricting and requires states to draw maps through independent citizen commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no action before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped states from redrawing congressional districts more than once every ten years, ending mid-decade remaps like the one Texas did in 2003. It would have required every state to draw its congressional map through an independent commission of ordinary citizens—people who had not held office or worked for a party or campaign in the previous four years—rather than letting legislators draw the lines. The commission could not consider voters' party affiliation, past voting behavior, or where incumbents live. All commission meetings and proposed maps would be public, with a website letting any citizen submit their own plan. If a state or its courts failed to produce a plan, a federal court would draw one. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters. Under the bill, congressional maps would be drawn by citizen commissions following open, public rules that bar consideration of party affiliation, voting history, and incumbent residences, and states could redraw districts only once per decade. That would take map-drawing power away from the politicians who benefit from safe districts and give voters a better chance of competitive elections, with a public website, open meetings, and the right to submit their own proposed maps [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary voters, and challengers to incumbents

how_it_helps.text: Each state would have to draw congressional districts through an independent commission whose members cannot have held office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the previous four years.

Commission members could not consider voters' party affiliation, voting history, or where incumbent House members live when drawing maps, so districts could not be engineered to protect a party or a sitting lawmaker.
A state could redraw its congressional map only once per decade, instead of after each census plus any mid-decade partisan remap like Texas's 2003 redistricting.

All commission meetings would be public, a public website would post census and election data with free mapping software so anyone could draft and submit their own plan, and proposed maps would be published at least seven days before going to the legislature.

analysis.who_pays: Sitting members of Congress and state legislative majorities of both parties. They would lose the power to draw their own district lines and to protect their seats; a repeat redistricting to lock in an advantage would be illegal except under court order, and the people drawing the lines could not be recent officeholders, candidates, or party employees [S3]. States would also take on the administrative cost of running commissions, offset by federal payments of $150,000 per House seat [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would override the choices of states that have adopted their own redistricting systems, replacing them with a single federal template rather than letting each state decide how to draw its congressional map.

Commission members would be appointed by the majority and minority leaders of each chamber of the state legislature, so the two major parties would still pick the people drawing the lines; the bill only bars those members from being recent officeholders, candidates, or party employees.

If a state legislature rejected the commission's plan and a state court failed to pick one, a federal district court would draw the map—putting unelected judges in charge of political boundaries as a fallback.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but diffuse: districts drawn without regard to incumbents or party registration would likely be more compact and competitive, and voters would get a public process with maps posted online and open meetings [S3]. The costs and risks: a one-size-federal-mandate approach overrides the different methods states have chosen for themselves, and the commission design still lets legislative leaders of both parties pick members, which does not fully remove political influence; court-drawn maps are also no guarantee of better representation [S3]. On balance the bill attacked a genuine structural problem—lawmakers drawing their own districts—with a workable if imperfect mechanism, and its death left that problem untouched.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Johnson introduced it alone, the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and the bill expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Johnson introduced the bill on June 24, 2009; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point in the two-year Congress.
The Judiciary Committee never reported the bill, no committee vote is recorded, and the full Senate never debated it; the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress and state legislative majorities of both parties, who kept the power to draw their own district lines without an independent commission or a ban on repeat redistricting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent lawmakers who kept their map-drawing power

for.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in June 2009; it was his first and only action on it in the record.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in June 2009 and took no recorded action—no hearing, no markup, no report—for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote or committee action ever occurred, and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured—though redistricting reform generally runs against the interest of legislators of both parties.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and legislative majorities of both parties
industries.note: The bill took map-drawing power away from the lawmakers it affects: no more protecting incumbents' homes, no more partisan gerrymanders, and no repeat redistricting between censuses. It also bars commission members from being recent officeholders, candidates, or party staff.

industries.industry: Political consultants and redistricting software vendors
industries.note: A ban on mid-decade remaps and a shift to citizen commissions would shrink the market for high-priced map-drawing expertise and partisan data work, though states would receive federal funds ($150,000 per House seat) to run their commissions.
